The statement is an unchanged theorem about arbitrary bipartite graphs, without identifying this board graph or its required output. Specialize it to the prime-ratio graph and state that its reached even-labelled vertices are exactly the winning initial selections.

Putting the even-endpoint costs specifically on cross-arcs fixes one encoding; equivalent networks can place those costs on endpoint arcs. Likewise, the Omega bookkeeping in H2 and auxiliary-loop bookkeeping in H5 belong with their respective reductions rather than among universal END constraints. H5's instruction to deduplicate prime divisors is unnecessarily restrictive: repeated adjacency entries can be harmless and need not be removed. review.editorial_note: None of the paths represents the reference algorithm's exact table through 83 followed by twice the largest prime at most n/3 for every n >= 84. The graph instead establishes a three-prime construction guaranteed from 177 and computes exceptional answers by matching-based methods. Moreover, the supplied editorial's perfect-matching characterization is false: deleting one vertex from an even-order board cannot leave a perfect matching, although such boards can have winning starts. N5's maximum-matching exposure characterization is the correct theorem; do not replace it with the editorial's assertion.
